ci: fix PR description check to use word count instead of line count
body:
## Summary

The description gate added in #6579 counted raw newline characters in the PR body text and required at least 10 of them. This looked reasonable in isolation, but it turned out to measure the wrong thing: GitHub stores a PR description as plain markdown text and only inserts a literal newline where the author actually pressed enter, then soft-wraps long paragraphs into many visual lines purely for display. A short, sparse bullet list with ten one-word items would pass this check easily, while a genuinely detailed, well-written explanation written as a few full paragraphs could fail it outright, purely because of formatting style rather than actual content or substance.

This was caught in practice on PR #6571, "Extract login-flow values from non-JSON responses via step regex," which has a thorough five-paragraph description explaining the change, its motivation, and two deviations forced by this branch. That description is 161 words long but only 5 raw lines, so it failed the old >=10 line requirement and blocked an otherwise well-documented PR.

## What changed

Replaced the line-count check in `pr-fast-checks.yml` with a word-count check requiring at least 100 words in the PR description, after stripping HTML comment boilerplate (e.g. PR template placeholder text). 100 words was chosen as roughly equivalent to the original "10 lines" intent, assuming typical prose density, while no longer penalizing paragraph-style writing versus bullet lists.

## Test plan
- [x] Verified PR #6571's actual 161-word description now passes the new threshold (confirmed locally before pushing)
- [x] Confirm this PR's own description, written here, passes `pr-fast-checks` once CI runs
- [ ] Spot check a deliberately short/low-effort description still correctly fails

feat: impossible travel via aggregation groupBy + distinct country
body:
## Impossible travel via the existing aggregation engine

Alert when **one identity** is seen from **N distinct countries** within a window, written as a plain YAML policy. No new detector.

```
request ─► identity = groupBy {source,key}   ── missing? ─► ignore rule
        └► value    = distinctIdentifier {attribute: country_code | source,key}
                         │
         aggKey = <identity>|<filterId>   (groupBy absent ⇒ <actor IP>|<filterId>, unchanged)
                         │
        WindowBasedThresholdNotifier.checkDistinct ─► distinct members in window ≥ count ?
                         │ yes
        event (AGGREGATED) + metadata.reason = "x-user-id=u1: 2 distinct country_code within 30 min (DE, FR)"
```

### Example policy: impossible travel

```yaml
id: ImpossibleTravel
filter:
  url:
    regex: ".*"

info:
  name: "ImpossibleTravel"
  description: "Detects one user identity being seen from multiple countries within a short window."
  details: "Requests are grouped by the user identity taken from the x-user-id request header. If the same identity is seen from 2 or more distinct countries (resolved from the source IP) within 30 minutes, an alert is raised. Requests without the identity header are ignored."
  impact: "A user appearing from different countries within minutes suggests a stolen session or credentials being used by someone else."
  category:
    name: "ImpossibleTravel"
    displayName: "Impossible Travel"
  subCategory: "Impossible Travel"
  severity: HIGH

aggregation_rules:
  - rule:
      name: "Rule 1"
      condition:
        windowThreshold: 30          # minutes
        groupBy:                     # whose behaviour is aggregated
          source: request_headers    # request_headers | request_payload | response_payload
          key: x-user-id
        distinctIdentifier:          # what is counted distinctly
          attribute: country_code
          count: 2                   # alert at 2 or more distinct countries
```

title: Add claimNextTestWork API:  Simplify mini-testing control loop, BE should be telling what needs to be done.
body:
## What changed

A new endpoint, `claimNextTestWork`, replaces four separate calls mini-testing used to make to pick up work. The old flow let a run get stuck: its summary (TRRS) ends up `FAILED` but the parent run stays `RUNNING` forever — the dashboard shows a spinner that never resolves. Real customer incident.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph before["Before: 4 calls, inconsistent state possible"]
        A1["findPendingTestingRunResultSummary"] --> A2["findPendingTestingRun"]
        A2 --> A3["createTRRSummaryIfAbsent"]
        A3 --> A4["claimTestingRunResultSummary"]
        A4 -.->|"a SCHEDULED run anywhere\nin the account blocks this"| A5["TRRS=FAILED,\nTestingRun=RUNNING forever"]
    end
    subgraph after["After: 1 atomic call"]
        B1["claimNextTestWork"] --> B2{"existing\nclaimable TRRS?"}
        B2 -->|yes| B3["claim it\n(CICD / RERUN / RECLAIMED_ABANDONED)"]
        B2 -->|no| B4{"bare due\nSCHEDULED run?"}
        B4 -->|yes| B5["flip it RUNNING,\nmint one TRRS (FRESH_RUN)"]
        B4 -->|no| B6["NO_WORK_FOUND"]
    end
```

## What it returns

One call, one of five verdicts telling the caller exactly which situation it picked up:

| Verdict | Fires when | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `FRESH_RUN` | No claimable summary exists; a due `SCHEDULED` run has none yet | Plain UI run or whole-test rerun — mints a new summary |
| `CICD` | A `SCHEDULED` summary exists with `metadata` set | Pre-created by a CI/CD trigger |
| `RERUN_SPECIFIC_TESTCASES` | A `SCHEDULED` summary exists with `originalTestingRunResultSummaryId` set | Pre-created for a "rerun specific testcases" job |
| `RECLAIMED_ABANDONED` | A `RUNNING` summary exists with an expired lease, or a lease token matching the caller's own | Previous worker died, or the caller is retrying its own still-valid claim |
| `NO_WORK_FOUND` | None of the above | Nothing to do |

That's the fix for the incident: previously the only way to tell which situation a run was in meant reconstructing it from raw Mongo state after the fact, which is what took hours during the original diagnosis.

Two contract notes for anyone building against this:
- Safe to retry with the same lease token after losing an HTTP response — won't be told someone else grabbed the work.
- The response always reflects the actually-persisted document.

## Tests

`TestClaimNextTestWork` — 21 cases: every verdict, the incident shape itself (unrelated `SCHEDULED` run must not block reclaim of an abandoned one), lease boundary conditions, and two concurrency tests proving the atomic claim never double-claims under 8 racing threads.

## Also fixed (test infra, pre-existing)

`mvn test` on this branch silently ran **zero** tests before this PR — two unrelated bugs in `pom.xml`/`libs/utils/pom.xml` made Surefire's test discovery fail before it ever reached a real test. Fixed both so this PR's tests (and the existing ones) actually run.

body:
## Summary
- Adds four GitHub Actions checks scoped to PRs targeting `feature/mini-runtime-release`, so they don't affect `master` or `feature/cyborg-release`:
  - **pr-size-check**: fails if a PR changes more than 1000 lines, excluding generated/vendor paths (`target/`, `node_modules/`, `dist/`, `build/`, lockfiles, `*.min.js`)
  - **pr-description-check**: fails if the PR description has fewer than 10 non-empty lines (HTML comment boilerplate is stripped first)
  - **pr-reviewer-comment-check**: fails unless at least one reviewer (not the author, not a bot) has left an actual non-empty comment — a bare approval/request-changes with no text does not count
  - **pr-coverage-check**: runs `mvn package -pl apps/mini-testing,apps/mini-runtime -am` on JDK 17, then uses `diff-cover` against the JaCoCo XML reports to require >=50% coverage on the lines the PR actually changed (patch coverage, not whole-repo coverage)

## Notes
- None of these are yet required status checks — branch protection on `feature/mini-runtime-release` needs to be configured separately (currently has none) to actually block merges on these.
- Tests for mini-testing/mini-runtime use `de.flapdoodle.embed.mongo`, so the coverage job runs self-contained without needing a live DB.

## Test plan
- [x] Open a throwaway PR against `feature/mini-runtime-release` to confirm all four checks trigger and report correctly
- [x] Verify pr-size-check correctly excludes a lockfile-only change
- [x] Verify pr-reviewer-comment-check fails on an approval with no comment text, passes once a real comment is added

title: Extract login-flow values from non-JSON responses via step regex
body:
Port of #6530 onto the mini-runtime release branch, extended to mini-testing so regex extraction also works during test runs.

The Regex field on a "Call API" login step was only ever read by the OTP node, so it was a no-op for API steps. populateRegexValues now applies it to the raw response body and exposes the result as <nodeId>.response.regex (first capture group, or the whole match when the regex has no groups) and <nodeId>.response.regex.N per group. This makes values that have no JSON path reachable, e.g. a CSRF token inside an HTML page.

Two deviations from the master version, both forced by this branch:
- plain null/trim check instead of StringUtils.isBlank, since this branch's copy of libs/utils Utils.java imports spring's StringUtils, which has no isBlank

title: Add weak authentication reason to malicious event metadata
body:
## Summary
WeakAuthentication threat events only said that auth was weak, not *why*. This adds a specific reason to the event metadata and shows it in the event details view.

Example (from a real event with a valid RS256 Bearer token and a stale session cookie):
`Expired JWT in cookie 'auth-session' (expired 1228s before detection)`

## Changes
**threat-detection**
- `ThreatDetector.getWeakAuthenticationReason()` returns a readable reason, or `null` if nothing is weak. `isWeakAuthenticationThreat()` now delegates to it, so what gets detected is unchanged.
- JWT reasons name the source (`Authorization Bearer token`, `cookie '<name>'`, `header '<name>'`) and include the `alg` for weak algorithms.
- `Utils.buildSampleMaliciousRequest` gains an overload that takes `reason` and sets it on `Metadata.reason`, a proto field that already existed but wasn't populated. The existing signature passes `null`, so other callers (Hyperscan, sequence anomaly) are untouched.
- Metadata is now attached when a reason exists even if geo `RawApiMetadata` is null. Previously it was dropped in that case.
- `MaliciousTrafficDetectorTask` sets the reason for the `WeakAuthentication` filter.

**dashboard**
- Event details (click a row, then the **Values** tab): a "Detection Reason" banner shows `metadata.reason`, next to the existing Schema Validation Errors banner in `SampleDataList`.
- The banner is opt-in through a new `showDetectionReason` prop, and only the threat event details (`SampleDetails`) passes it, so other `SampleDataList` users (testing, guardrail violations) are unaffected. It renders only in the API Security category: guardrails-service also writes `metadata.reason`, and those events keep their existing views.
- No new table column. Events without a reason show no banner.

No backend or proto changes: `metadata` is already stored as a string and turned into JSON for the dashboard.

## Notes
- Reasons deliberately avoid `": "`, because `parseStoredReason` strips any prefix before the first `": "`. A test enforces this.
- Only WeakAuthentication events detected after deploy carry a reason. Existing events and other filters show no banner.

## Backward compatibility
- `Metadata.reason` (field 6) already existed in the proto, so there are no schema or wire changes. Older consumers ignore it.
- The existing `buildSampleMaliciousRequest` signature is kept and delegates with `reason = null`, so Hyperscan and sequence-anomaly events are byte-for-byte unchanged.
- `isWeakAuthenticationThreat` returns the same results: all 29 pre-existing tests pass unchanged.
- UI, checked locally against real backend responses: an old event with no `reason` (metadata `{"countryCode":"IN"}`) shows no banner and the Values tab renders as before, an event with empty metadata shows no banner and no error, and the table has no new column.

## Testing
- `WeakAuthenticationThreatTest`: 38 tests pass (29 existing, 9 new covering reason text, cookie/header naming, and the no-`": "` rule).
- Local end-to-end run:
  - The real detector code ran on the production request.
  - The event was posted to `record_malicious_event` on a local threat-detection-backend, went through Kafka and FlushMessagesToDB into `malicious_events`, and came back from `list_malicious_requests` with `{"reason": "..."}`.
  - In the local dashboard, clicking the event in API Threat Activity and opening Values shows the Detection Reason banner with the full text, and the table has no extra column. The dashboard's event list and details fetches were answered with the local backend's real responses, because the local dashboard reads threat data from the hosted backend.

Export all rows from server tables, not just the first backend page
body:
## Problem
The **Export as CSV** button on server-side tables only exported the first page the backend returned. The table asked for every row in one request, but many backends cap rows per request (Endpoint Shield caps at 200; others at 50, 200 or 500), so the CSV was cut off.

## Fix
One change in `GithubServerTable.js` (`handleExportCsv`):
- The first request goes out as before. If it comes back with fewer rows than the total, the export keeps fetching with `skip = k × firstPageSize` (the same stepping the table's own pagination uses) until it reaches the total.
- Rows are de-duplicated by `id`, and a page that adds no new rows ends the loop. Tables whose fetch ignores `skip` therefore can't produce duplicates or loop forever.
- Filters are cloned for each request, because some pages mutate the filters object inside `fetchData`.
- After a multi-page export, the visible page is re-fetched. This restores the loading state and row caches that the extra fetches overwrote.

Tables without a backend cap, and client-side tables, still make a single request, so they're unchanged.

litellm hook: quarantine blocked prompts per text block so one block does not lock the whole Claude Code session
body:
## Problem

With the LiteLLM hook in `SYNC_MODE`, one blocked prompt in Claude Code causes every later prompt in the same session to be blocked.

When a request is blocked, Claude Code doesn't start a new turn. It appends the user's next prompt to the rejected message as another text block. The verdict judges "the newest user turn", which still contains the blocked text, so Akto blocks it again. The existing quarantine couldn't help, for two reasons:
- `strip_quarantined_history` never touches the newest user turn.
- It only ran after an allowed verdict, which never happens in this state.

Observed against a live tenant (one Claude Code session, `Malicious-Tools` / `PromptInjection` policy):

| Prompt typed | Text sent for verdict (before this PR) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `Reply with exactly: ok` | `Reply with exactly: ok` | Blocked |
| `What is 2+2?` | `Reply with exactly: ok What is 2+2?` | Blocked |
| `What is the capital of France?` | `Reply with exactly: ok What is 2+2? What is the capital of France?` | Blocked |

## Change (`apps/mcp-endpoint-shield/litellm/custom_hooks.py`)

- **Remember per text block.** `remember_blocked` stores one key per text block of the blocked turn, with harness `<system-reminder>` blocks excluded. It used to store the whole turn.
- **Strip before judging.** `validate_and_block` now calls `strip_quarantined_history` **before** the verdict, not after an allowed one. The verdict judges only new content, and the model never sees rejected text.
- **Strip blocks from every user turn, the newest included.**
  - A turn left with no content is dropped, together with the assistant reply that followed it, as before.
  - A newest turn made only of blocked text is left unchanged, so it's judged (and blocked) again rather than forwarded empty.
  - Plain-string turns are still quarantined as a whole.
- **Short texts.** Texts under `QUARANTINE_MIN_CHARS` (12) now match only exactly. Before, they were never tracked, so a short blocked prompt such as `Say hello` could never be quarantined.
- **Unused helper removed.** `_fingerprint` is replaced by `_fingerprints`. `_normalize` is shared by the matching helpers.

Unchanged: quarantine is still in-memory, per LiteLLM process and per session id, and gated by `QUARANTINE_BLOCKED_HISTORY`.

## Testing

- **New unit tests:** `tests/quarantine/test_quarantine.py`, 12 tests. They cover a merged newest turn, harness blocks, re-judging a resent blocked prompt, dropping or trimming earlier turns, containment matching, exact matching for short texts, plain-string turns, session isolation and the disable flag, plus an end-to-end `validate_and_block` replay of the Claude Code sequence.
  - All 12 pass with this change.
  - Against the previous `custom_hooks.py`, 5 of them fail (4 failures, 1 error).
  - Run inside the LiteLLM image: `python -m unittest discover -s tests/quarantine -v` from `apps/mcp-endpoint-shield/litellm`.
- **Live test:** Claude Code → LiteLLM (`main-latest`, 1.104.0) with this hook → Akto guardrails, all in one session.
  - `Reply with exactly: ok` is still blocked.
  - The follow-up prompts are answered ("2 + 2 = 4, and the capital of France is Paris").
  - The request logged at `async_log_success_event` contains only the new prompts, without the blocked text.

title: Fence terminal-state writes on lease, fix countTestingRunResultSummaries serialization
body:
## Root cause

`countTestingRunResultSummaries` crashed client-side with `CodecConfigurationException`
before ever sending its request — a raw `Bson` query-builder object was handed to
`BasicDBObject.toString()`, which has no codec for it. The old signature never worked
for any caller. The crash's own fallthrough had no guard preventing a run from being
marked complete with no summary ever established, which is what caused a real
production incident: a partially-complete `TestingRun` got marked `COMPLETED`.

Paired with the client-side fix on `feat/stateless-mini-testing` (PR #6451).

## Changes

- `countTestingRunResultSummaries`: raw `Bson filter` → primitives
  (`testingRunHexId`, `sinceTimestamp`, `state`). Clean replacement, not additive —
  nothing ever depended on the old signature working. Also added the try/catch this
  action was missing entirely.
- New shared `claimableOrOwnedByFilter(leaseToken)`: matches when a document has no
  valid current owner (never leased, or lease expired) or the caller's token matches
  the current owner. Claim/reclaim-shaped only — documented as not for renewal-shaped
  writes (periodic count increments, `markProducerDone`, lease extension), which must
  match the current owner exactly.
- `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed` / `updateIssueCountInSummaryFenced`: new
  leaseToken-fenced overloads, closing the gap where a stale caller arriving via the
  lease-blind discovery fallback could mark FAILED/COMPLETED on an attempt a
  different, currently-active owner holds. Original unconditional signatures kept for
  backward compatibility with not-yet-upgraded clients.
- `DataActor`/`DbActor` mirrored for interface compliance.
- Removed the now-dead `Bson filter` field/setter on `DbAction`, unused after the
  signature change above.

## Out of scope, deliberately

- A few other unfenced terminal-write call sites exist on the client side
  (`markTestingRunFailed` alone, `updateTestRunResultSummaryNoUpsert`,
  `updateIssueCountAndStateInSummary`, and one call site in `TestRateLimitGuard.java`
  that would need `leaseToken` threaded through the per-API-test execution engine).
  Same risk class, different trigger paths not reopened by this PR — fast-follow.

title: Stamp lease on the original summary for the rerun case
body:
## What

The rerun feature (re-run a specific selected `TestingRunResult`) claims a throwaway summary to get a valid lease token, then drains a *different* document — the original, already-`COMPLETED` summary the selected result belongs to (`getOriginalTestingRunResultSummaryId()`). The lease claim/adopt cycle only ever stamped `leaseToken`/`leaseExpiryTs` onto the throwaway summary; nothing stamped it on the original one before draining began.

## Root cause, confirmed live

Every rerun attempt self-fenced with `LEASE_LOST` within ~20-25s:
```
Lease lost while draining summary <original>; no longer safe to run unfenced.
why=another module's claim was accepted - this pod's token was rejected
```
Every write during the drain (renewal, the single result recording) CAS'd against `(summaryId=original, leaseToken=<fresh token>)`, which could never match — the original summary's own `leaseToken` field was still whatever it had been left at by its *original* run, up to 23+ hours stale in testing, completely unrelated to the token the rerun attempt had just adopted.

## Fix

`updateStartTsTestRunResultSummary` is already the existing, correctly-timed hook for this — called once, right after a rerun confirms it has real work to do, before draining starts. Extended it to also accept the caller's lease token and, when present, stamp it onto the summary alongside flipping `state` back to `RUNNING` (from `COMPLETED`) — reopening it as a genuinely valid, lease-protected target for the drain that follows.

The existing completion path (`Main.java`'s post-init `markTestAsComplete`, gated on the lease *not* being lost) then transitions it back to `COMPLETED` naturally once the drain finishes — no new completion logic needed, it was just never reached before because every attempt hit `LEASE_LOST` first.

## Backward compatibility

`leaseToken` is nullable — empty/absent falls through to exactly the old unconditional timestamp-only update. A not-yet-upgraded mini-testing client (old 1-arg call, no token) continues working against this server unchanged.

## Verification

Verified live end-to-end against real local data:
- Lease correctly stamped (fresh token, ~360s expiry, `state: RUNNING`)
- Zero `LEASE_LOST`
- `TESTRUN END reason=ALL_PROCESSED`
- The selected result's stale document deleted and replaced with a fresh one reflecting the rerun's actual outcome
- The original summary's `testResultsCount`/`countIssues` correctly incremented

Companion client-side change (passing the token through): akto-api-security/akto-mini-runtime#6451

title: Add producerDone and lease fields to TestingRunResultSummary + migration
body:
## Why

Schema half of the stateless mini-testing work, ported to `master` so the DTO doesn't diverge and so customer environments pick up the index on upgrade.

mini-testing resumed an interrupted test run from `TestingStateStore` — a JSON file on the pod's own filesystem. A replaced container loses that file, so the run fell through to reclaim, which fails the summary and re-executes everything from scratch. These fields move that state onto the summary itself, where any module can read it.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `producerDone` | every message of the attempt has reached Kafka, so the work set is complete and can be resumed rather than re-produced |
| `leaseExpiryTs` | when the current owner's claim lapses |
| `leaseToken` | minted per claim, so a module that restarts and re-claims fences out its own previous threads |

Behaviour lives in the other two PRs — server #6450, client #6451. Nothing on `master` reads these fields yet.

## Why primitives

An `ObjectId`- or `Date`-typed field here gets bean-introspected into `{"timestamp": N, "date": "..."}` by the abstractor's Struts JSON layer, and plain Jackson then silently rebuilds it client-side by calling `ObjectId`'s no-arg constructor — which mints a brand new valid id rather than failing. That's the failure mode fixed in #6444, and it's the reason all three are `boolean`/`int`/`String`.

## The migration

`findPendingTestingRunResultSummary` filters on `leaseExpiryTs` in a polling loop, and without an index that branch of the `$or` scans the collection. The changeset mirrors the index added to `TestingRunResultSummariesDao.createIndicesIfAbsent`.

**Sparse**, because only summaries currently owned by a module carry the field — a single-field sparse index omits the rest, keeping it to the handful of in-flight runs rather than every summary ever recorded.

**No backfill, deliberately.** Summaries written before the lease existed have no `leaseExpiryTs`, and a mongo range predicate does not match a missing field. That's load-bearing, not an oversight: backfilling would make those summaries match the reclaim filter, and they belong to modules that never renew a lease — so it would let a module reclaim its own still-running work. The reclaim query keeps its original wall-clock branch to serve them instead.

## Risk

Additive only. No existing reader or writer touches these fields, the index is created if absent and dropped on rollback, and no data is rewritten.

title: Resume test runs from mongo and kafka instead of a local file
body:
## Why

Mini-testing resumed an interrupted run from `TestingStateStore` — a JSON file on the pod's own filesystem. That made resumption work only for a pod whose disk survived. When a container is replaced it doesn't, so the run fell through to reclaim, which fails the summary, mints a replacement and re-runs everything from scratch. This is what the aba incident hit.

This is the **client half**. Server half: akto#6450, which must ship first.

## What moves where

The file held seven keys. Four already had working fallbacks in `ConsumerUtil.init` and simply go away — `accountId`, `testRunMaxTimeSeconds`, `pickedUpTimestamp`, `testingRunId`. The other three are the load-bearing ones:

| key | was | now |
|---|---|---|
| `summaryId` | no fallback — `init()` returned immediately without it | the claim itself returns the attempt |
| `consumerRunning` | default false, which skipped the whole poll loop | `producerDone` on the summary |
| `expectedRecords` | default -1, which disabled the completion check | Kafka consumer-group lag |

## Why lag, and not just moving expectedRecords to mongo

`expectedRecords` was compared against `processedRecords` — an `AtomicInteger` that restarts at **zero on every `init()`**. A resumed drain could never reach the total however much work was genuinely left, so it spun until max runtime. Moving the target to mongo wouldn't fix that; the counter is the broken half.

Lag is absolute rather than a delta from process start, so a fresh process reads the same truth as the one that died. A committed offset also *means the test ran* — the parallel consumer only advances an offset once the record's handler returns, and the handler blocks on the test future.

It's also honest about what it doesn't know: unreadable lag is `-1` and never treated as zero, since a broker hiccup must not look like completion.

## Resume stops being a separate code path

It used to run *before* the `while` loop, because only the pod that wrote the file could read it. Once the trigger is a query, restart and takeover are the same thing — so resume is just what the loop does when it claims a summary whose production already finished.

That also closes an ordering trap: a resumable attempt would otherwise be handed to the reclaim block and failed, discarding the very work it came back to finish.

`producerDone` is the commit point that makes every crash window safe:

- **false** ⇒ consumption never started ⇒ no results exist ⇒ the partial topic is disposable, so re-produce (`initProducer`'s delete-on-entry is what makes this correct, and is deliberately kept).
- **true** ⇒ the work set is complete ⇒ resume consuming via `doInitOnly`, which skips that delete.

## The lease

Makes the above safe with more than one pod. The token is minted **per claim, not per pod**, so a module that restarts and re-claims fences out its own previous threads by the same mechanism that fences a different module.

Renewal rides writes that already happen — per result while draining, and the produce loop during fan-out, which writes no results and would otherwise lapse mid-production. **Renewing from the thread doing the work is deliberate:** a background timer would keep the lease alive for a pod wedged mid-request, which is exactly the pod that should lose it.

Two mutations become owner-only, because both destroy a live run when performed by a superseded pod that woke up: deleting the attempt's Kafka topic, and marking the run complete.

## LeaseStatus: rejected ≠ failed

Collapsing the two — what every other `DataActor` call does by swallowing to null — would make a transient abstractor blip abandon a healthy run.

`UNKNOWN` needs no retry policy or failure counting, because it decays into rejection by arithmetic: a lease not renewed within its TTL has expired server-side whether or not we heard back. A pod partitioned from the abstractor therefore stands down on its own.

## Compatibility

Against an old abstractor that doesn't send `leaseHeld`, `parseLeaseStatus` yields `APPLIED` — so a new client keeps working exactly as it does today. Against the new one, leasing engages. `CONCURRENT_TESTING` is untouched and still off; per-summary topics remain a customer-side switch.

## Not addressed here

`testResultsCount` still double-counts on redelivery — fencing can't fix that, since the redelivering pod *is* the legitimate owner; it needs a per-message idempotency key. The global SCHEDULED starvation gate in `findPendingTestingRunResultSummary` is a separate pre-existing bug.

title: Add lease and producerDone to TestingRunResultSummary for stateless mini-testing resumption
body:
## Why

Mini-testing resumes an interrupted test run from `TestingStateStore` — a JSON file on the pod's local filesystem. That is the *only* resume mechanism, and it fails whenever the filesystem doesn't survive (container replacement, node move, fresh pod). When it fails, the run is only recoverable through the reclaim path, which mints a new summary and re-runs everything from scratch, discarding all completed work.

This is the **server half** of relocating that state into Mongo so any pod can resume, plus a lease so two pods cannot own the same attempt. The client half follows in a mini-runtime PR; this one ships first and is a no-op until a client opts in.

## Schema

Three fields on `TestingRunResultSummary`:

| field | purpose |
|---|---|
| `boolean producerDone` | production finished, so the Kafka work set is complete and a pod may resume consuming instead of re-producing |
| `int leaseExpiryTs` | when the current owner's claim lapses |
| `String leaseToken` | minted fresh per claim, so a restarted pod fences out its own previous threads |

All primitives, deliberately. An `ObjectId`- or `Date`-typed field gets bean-introspected by Struts into `{timestamp, date}`, which plain Jackson then silently mints a fresh value for client-side — the bug fixed in #6444.

No `DaoInit` change (the class rides `.automatic(true)`, which needs both accessor halves — provided). No migration.

## The compatibility contract

Cyborg ships first; mini-testing upgrades on the customer's schedule, possibly never. **Old clients must keep working indefinitely.** Two facts make the obvious approach unsafe:

1. **A mongo range predicate does not match a missing field.** Every summary already in Mongo lacks `leaseExpiryTs`, so replacing the wall-clock window with `leaseExpiryTs < now` would make all of them permanently unreclaimable.
2. **Old clients never renew.** A lease stamped on their claim would expire mid-run, and the same module's next poll would reclaim its own live run and mint a replacement — a worse regression than the bug being fixed.

So the reclaim filter is **additive**, not a replacement:

```
state == RUNNING AND (
    (startTimestamp <= now-300 AND startTimestamp > delta)   // unchanged
 OR (leaseExpiryTs < now)                                    // new, no age bound
)
```

and **a lease is only stamped when the request carries a token**. No token ⇒ today's behaviour, byte for byte. That is one null check rather than a parallel code path.

The payoff: unlike the window, the lease branch has no upper age bound, so an attempt stranded for hours stays recoverable. Old clients keep the 20-minute visibility ceiling they have today.

## Also fixed here

The three TRRS claim sites filtered on `_id` alone — no state predicate — so two modules racing both received a non-null summary and both proceeded. They collapse into one `claimTestingRunResultSummary` helper that CASes properly. The helper returns the **pre-update** document: callers branch on the state the summary had *before* the claim (the `state == SCHEDULED` GitHub-status branch in mini-testing's `Main`), so returning the post-image would silently kill that branch for every client. The lease fields are attached to the pre-image afterwards so the caller still learns its token.

## Renewal without a heartbeat

Lease renewal rides `updateTestResultsCountInTestSummary`, which already runs once per result. `bulkRecordTestingRunResults` calls straight through that same method, so both write paths renew and fence for free — no new endpoint, no background job.

## leaseHeld is in the body, not the status code

Losing a lease is a domain outcome, not a transport failure. Struts maps an action ERROR to 422, which a client cannot distinguish from the abstractor being unwell — and that exact conflation is what turned an earlier NPE on this path into an indefinitely stuck test run. Note this required changing `excludeProperties=.*` on two routes, which were returning an empty body.

## Risk

Zero behaviour change for any client that doesn't send `leaseToken`. Verified by construction: every new predicate and every new write is behind a non-empty token check. Rollback is a revert; the three fields are additive and ignored by readers that don't know them.

title: Fix ObjectId fabrication in fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap (root cause of stuck test runs)
body:
## What

Root-cause fix for mini-testing runs getting permanently stuck after a pod crash mid-execution, on the client side. Companion PR to [akto#6444](https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6444), which made the equivalent server-side fixes.

## Root cause

`ObjectId` fields (`id`, `testingRunId`) don't survive a Struts2 JSON response -> plain Jackson round trip intact:

- Struts2 has no special case for `ObjectId`, so it falls back to bean-introspecting it into `{"timestamp": N, "date": "..."}` instead of a hex string.
- Plain Jackson (this client's `objectMapper`) can't bind that shape back onto an `ObjectId` field. Rather than throwing, its generic fallback constructs the target type via its no-arg constructor — and `ObjectId()`'s no-arg constructor doesn't mean "empty", it actively **mints a brand-new, valid, completely unrelated ObjectId**.

No exception, no null — and every other (scalar-typed) field on the same object deserializes correctly in the same call, which is what made this so easy to miss.

## Why only this one method

Every other `TestingRunResultSummary`-returning method in `ClientActor` (`findPendingTestingRunResultSummary`, `createTRRSummaryIfAbsent`, etc.) already goes through `parseTestingRunResultSummaryFromResponsePayload`, which strips the raw `id`/`testingRunId` fields *before* Jackson ever sees them and rebuilds both from the plain-String `hexId`/`testingRunHexId` mirror fields instead — a shape both serializers round-trip correctly. `fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` was the one method that called `objectMapper.readValue` directly on the raw response with no such guard.

## Why this mattered

This was the confirmed root cause of the stuck-run incident: `Main.java`'s recovery loop calls `fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` to look up an orphaned run's summary, then uses that summary's id for every subsequent lookup (`fetchLatestTestingRunResult`, `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed`, etc.) — but the id it received was fabricated, so every lookup silently targeted a document that never existed. Confirmed live: captured the real response from `ultron.akto.io` for a completed run and reproduced the exact fabrication with the real `com.akto.dto.testing.TestingRunResultSummary` class and this exact deserialization code.

## Changes

- Extracted the strip-and-rebuild logic from `parseTestingRunResultSummaryFromResponsePayload` into a shared `parseTestingRunResultSummary(BasicDBObject)` helper.
- `fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` now calls that helper per map entry instead of bulk-parsing the raw map directly with Jackson.
- `TestingRun.getHexId()` and `TestingRunResultSummary.getHexId()`/`getTestingRunHexId()` now prefer the transmitted hex string field over recomputing from the `ObjectId`, matching the companion server-side fix in akto#6444 — defense in depth for any other caller that still ends up with a corrupted `ObjectId` field.
- `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed` now recognizes HTTP 404 (the companion server-side change: no matching `RUNNING` summary found) and logs it distinctly from a generic non-2xx error.

## No Main.java changes

Deliberately not touching `Main.java`: with `fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` fixed at the source, every existing `.getId()`/`.getHexId()` call site there already produces correct results — the bug was entirely in how the response was parsed, not in how the resulting object was used. (`findPendingTestingRun`'s `TestingRun` and `findPendingTestingRunResultSummary`'s `trrs` were both already safe via their own existing parsing guards — confirmed by reading each, not assumed.)

## Compatibility

Client-only change, no wire format change. Depends on the server (akto#6444) for the 404-specific logging to trigger — until that's deployed, `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed` still returns 422 for this case and this client falls through to the existing generic-error logging path, so this PR is safe to deploy independently of akto#6444's rollout order.

title: Fix getHexId() ObjectId fabrication and the NPE it exposed in markTestRunResultSummaryFailed
body:
## What

Two fixes, together closing out the root cause of mini-testing runs getting permanently stuck after a pod crash mid-execution.

## Fix 1 — `getHexId()` silently fabricating ObjectIds (the root cause)

`TestingRun.getHexId()` and `TestingRunResultSummary.getHexId()`/`getTestingRunHexId()` unconditionally recomputed from their `ObjectId` field instead of preferring the separately-transmitted plain-String hex field. Brought in line with the pattern already used correctly by `TestingRunResult`'s three hex getters and `TestingRunResultSummary.getOriginalTestingRunResultSummaryHexId()`.

**Root cause:** `ObjectId` has no special case in either JSON layer on this path:
- **Struts2's `DefaultJSONWriter`** (server) has no case for `ObjectId`, so it falls through to generic bean-introspection, serializing it as `{"timestamp": N, "date": "..."}` (the only two JavaBean-style getters `ObjectId` exposes) instead of a hex string.
- **Plain Jackson** (client, `ClientActor`'s `objectMapper`) has no idea what to do with that object shape for an `ObjectId`-typed field. Rather than throwing, its generic fallback constructs the target type via its no-arg constructor — and `ObjectId()`'s no-arg constructor doesn't mean "empty", it actively **mints a brand-new, valid, completely unrelated ObjectId**.

Every `ObjectId` field that crosses from a Struts2 JSON response into a plain-Jackson client comes back silently fabricated — no exception, no null, and every other (scalar-typed) field on the same object deserializes correctly in the same call, which is what made this so easy to miss.

Confirmed live: captured the real response from `POST /fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` on ultron.akto.io for a completed run, then reproduced the exact fabrication using the real `com.akto.dto.testing.TestingRunResultSummary` class and `ClientActor`'s exact deserialization code — confirmed the root cause before writing the fix, not the other way around.

```java
public String getHexId() {
    if (hexId == null) return this.id.toHexString();
    return this.hexId;
}
```

## Fix 2 — NullPointerException in `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed`

`DbLayer.markTestRunResultSummaryFailed` does a conditional Mongo update guarded on the summary's state being `RUNNING`, and returns `null` (not an exception) when that filter matches zero documents. The next line dereferenced that result unconditionally:

```
NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "TestingRunResultSummary.getTestingRunId()" because "this.trrs" is null
```

Confirmed live in production — 10/10 calls, 100% failure rate, via the abstractor's own application log during the incident. Struts2 maps this method's uncaught-exception `ERROR` result to HTTP 422, which `ClientActor` treats as "some other thread already handled it" and moves on — so instead of surfacing as an error, this silently prevented the caller from ever closing out an orphaned run, compounding into an indefinite stuck loop with no alert.

Fix: return the existing `ERROR` result immediately when `trrs` is null, instead of crashing on the next line, and log the specific reason (`"No matching RUNNING summary found for markTestRunResultSummaryFailed, testingRunResultSummaryId=..."`) instead of a bare NPE stack trace. No response-shape change, no new result/status code — matches the standard `ERROR`/422 pattern every other action in this file already uses. Client-observable behavior on the no-match path is unchanged.

## Why together

Fix 1 removes one confirmed, reproduced cause of `markTestRunResultSummaryFailed`'s conditional update never matching (a fabricated summary id handed in by the client). Fix 2 makes the method itself safe regardless of *why* the match fails — including the genuinely benign race the caller already handles correctly. Neither fully explains the incident without the other: fix 1 alone still leaves a crash-on-legitimate-no-match landmine; fix 2 alone stops the crash but a run could still never be found under its real id.

## Compatibility

No wire format changes, no coordinated client/server deploy required for either fix. Fix 1: the server already emits a correct `hexId` value today (via bean-introspection of these exact getters at serialization time) — this only fixes what a client does with that value after re-parsing. Fix 2: doesn't change the response shape on success, and preserves the exact client-observable behavior on the no-match path. Safe against version skew in either direction.

## Companion PR

[akto-mini-runtime#6446](https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6446) is the client-side companion fix — the actual root cause of the fabricated ids (`ClientActor.fetchTestingRunResultSummaryMap` skipping the same parsing guard every other method already had). Neither PR depends on the other's rollout order.

## Not in scope here

The underlying structural risk this bug class stems from — two independent JSON serializers (Struts2 server-side, Jackson client-side) with no shared contract or codec for non-trivial types — is a separate, larger discussion. This PR fixes the specific getters and the specific crash that were the confirmed, reproduced cause of one production incident; it doesn't eliminate the possibility of a similar mismatch for some other type in the future.

title: Add jetty-context.xml for internal service configuration and update Dockerfile
body:
## RCA + fix: `akto-internal` OOM crash-loop filling the dashboard VM disk

### Root cause

`akto-internal` was OOM-killed on nearly every boot (`RestartCount=23`, `OOMKilled=true`, kills ~10s apart in `dmesg`). Jetty only deletes its unpacked-WAR scratch directory on a **graceful** shutdown i.e. `SIGKILL` can't be trapped, so every crash orphaned a ~108MB directory under `/tmp` in the container's writable layer.

Why it OOM'd: the JVM sat at **195MB anon inside a 200MB cap** before serving a single request. A heap histogram showed the memory going to Jetty's startup annotation scan - **46,918 `JarFileResource` + 47,711 `URL` + 178,434 char arrays (38MB)** , from bytecode-scanning all 213 bundled jars for annotations this app doesn't use (everything is declared in `web.xml`).

Not a leak: memory was flat over time, and a Full GC moved tenured only 80,175K → 77,584K.

### The fix

One new file (`apps/internal/jetty-context.xml`), wired in with one `COPY`:

| Setting | Fixes |
|---|---|
| `tempDirectory` → fixed path | Jetty unpacks to one fixed folder instead of a new random `/tmp` folder per boot |
| `WebInfIncludeJarPattern=^$` | Skips annotation-scanning `WEB-INF/lib` (unused here; no classes are removed, loading stays lazy) |

### Benchmarks `mem_limit: 200m`

| Metric | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| anon memory (idle) | 195 MB (98% of cap) | **110 MB (55%)** | **−44%** |
| anon memory (20-concurrent × 3 burst) | OOM-killed | **142 MB (71%)** | 58 MB headroom |
| annotation scan | 1885 ms | **9 ms** | **210× faster** |
| startup | 3858 ms | **1152 ms** | **3.3× faster** |
| orphaned dirs after 2 OOM-kills | 2, unbounded growth | **0** | leak eliminated |
| restarts under load | crash loop (23+) | **0** | stable |

title: Add metrics for avg payload, break down test cost more. Cache pattern compile, samples parsing
body:
## What

Replaces the profiler-dependent `OTHER = RUN_TEST − SEND_REQUEST` subtraction with explicit, always-on stage timers, fixes real defects found while using them on live customer infra, and ships three independently-measured perf fixes.

## Instrumentation

Mirrors the existing `TestPhaseTimer`/`SEND_REQUEST` pattern, wired at call sites confirmed against actual captured flamegraphs:

- **FILTER** — wraps `TestPlugin.validateFilter` in `YamlTestTemplate.filter()`
- **WORDLIST** — wraps `VariableResolver.resolveDynamicWordList` in `Executor.execute()`
- **VALIDATE** — wraps `Executor.validate()` at both call sites
- `TestRunMetrics`'s `TESTRUN COST` line reports named percentages for all four; residual `OTHER` is `RUN_TEST` minus all of them
- Added `avgPayloadKb`/`maxPayloadKb` to every `TESTRUN PROGRESS`/`STALL`/`END` line

**Fixed a real attribution bug found while using this in anger**: all four timers were `long t = nanoTime(); call(); addX(nanoTime()-t)` — if the wrapped call threw (a timed-out/interrupted send, a failing filter/validate), the recording line was skipped and that call's real elapsed time silently misattributed to `OTHER`. Confirmed live via jattach: 100/100 workers blocked inside the exact span `SEND_REQUEST` measures while its reported average stayed near-zero. All four sites now use `try/finally` so elapsed time is recorded regardless of outcome.

## Lock fix

`fetchOrFindTestRole` and `modifyAuthTokenInRawApi` were both `synchronized static`, sharing `Executor.class`'s monitor purely by accident (no invariant requires a role-fetch and a token-refresh to mutually exclude). Measured via JFR: 9,065s of aggregate thread-blocking time in one run; via live jstack: up to 42/100 workers piled on the identical lock address simultaneously.

- `fetchOrFindTestRole` → `ConcurrentHashMap.compute()`, per-role-name single-flight instead of a class-wide lock. All original semantics preserved (60s throttle, serve-stale-on-failure, and the keep-old-object merge that protects a warm auth token from being discarded by an unrelated definition refresh).
- `modifyAuthTokenInRawApi`'s lock moved inside the method, keyed per role name on a separate `authLocks` map. Also fixes a real gap — the `runOperation` call site had no lock wrapper at all; locking inside the method now covers it.

Verified post-fix: lock-wait threads collapsed from a steady 34-42/snapshot to 0-1, confirmed three independent ways (jstack, JFR, asprof — role-lock share 7.4% → 0.7% of execution-path time).

## STALL log now names the actual stuck thread

`TESTRUN STALL`'s `oldestTasks` always showed `thread=<pc-pool-N-thread-M>` — the Kafka-consumer callback thread that submitted the task, not the `mini-test-worker` executing it. jstack'ing that name is a dead end: it's always `TIMED_WAITING` on `FutureTask.get()`, never the real stuck call, because that name is captured inside the `poll()` callback before the worker pool even sees the task. Confirmed on two different customer accounts on live infra — a structural gap, not a one-off.

Fix: `runTestFromMessage` now takes the `recordId` and records the real worker thread name from inside itself, on the worker thread. `oldestTasks` now prints both `worker=<name>` (jstack this one) and `caller=<name>` (kept for cross-checking against the "picked up record" log line).

## Perf fixes

- **Pattern compile cache** (`checkIfContainsMatch`) — regex reused ~4.8M times/pass across ~428 distinct patterns, was recompiled every call.
- **Sample parsing cache** (`VariableResolver`) — payload parsed once, reused across wordlist checks instead of per-check.
- **`.*` fast path** (`checkIfContainsMatch`) — short-circuits the exact literal `.*` (a structural "match any" placeholder from `for_one`/`for_all` loops) to `true` without compiling/scanning. Measured at 41.6% of all match calls. Measured effect: `cpuPerTestMs` 54ms→36ms (-33%), throughput ~105/s→~119/s on a controlled run.

## Additional per-test cost fixes (dead logging, redundant fetch, uncached lookup)

Found and proven via JFR wall-clock sampling + full stack traces on a live customer run, then measured before/after with the same methodology used throughout this PR:

- **Removed 4 `logger.info` calls** (`AgenticUtils.isCopilotBotCollection`/`isLiteLLMAgent`, `ApiExecutorUtil.calculateHashAndAddAuth`) that sit behind SLF4J `SimpleLogger`'s global synchronized lock — proven via wall-clock sampling to be the single largest CPU/wall-clock consumer among worker threads under concurrent load, unrelated to payload size. One of the removed calls (`isCopilotBotCollection`) built a `Collectors.joining` tag-string unconditionally on every call regardless of whether the message would even be logged.
- **`workflow_node_executor/Utils.processNode`**: `fetchRecordedLoginFlowInput()` was called unconditionally on every graph/workflow node, but the result is only used for `RECORDED`-type nodes — `OTP`/`API` nodes fetched and immediately discarded it. Now fetched lazily. Measured on a real customer run: 24,827 calls → 0 for that run's node mix.
- **New `ApiInfoMetaCache`**, same pattern as the already-accepted `ApiCollectionMetaCache`: `FilterAction.applyFilterOnAccessType` and the `API_GROUP` membership check both called `dataActor.fetchApiInfo(apiInfoKey)` uncached, once per test, per call site. Scoped to one testing run (cleared from `TestingConfigurations.init()`) rather than the whole JVM lifetime, since — unlike `ApiCollectionMetaCache`'s tags, set once at discovery and never refreshed — `ApiInfo`'s access-type classification and API-group membership genuinely change between runs, and mini-testing is long-lived across many runs (`Main.java`'s `runModule` polls for pending runs in a loop).

## Root-caused, not fixed here (template issue, not code)

The `stuckSlots`/300s-timeout symptom chased through this investigation turned out to be neither the lock nor a slow target server, but **catastrophic regex backtracking**: `SourceCodeDisclosureWebInf.yaml`'s and `BigRedirectsScan.yml`'s own validate patterns (`.*java.*`, `.*href.*href.*`) hit Java regex's O(n²) worst case under `find()` when no match exists in a large (~64-69KB) payload — confirmed via a targeted temporary diagnostic (7.3-7.5s per single call). `find()` is already unanchored, so the leading/trailing `.*` in both patterns is redundant overhead with no functional purpose. Fix belongs in the template library (drop the redundant wrapping), not engine code — flagging here since it fully explains the tail-latency symptom this investigation started with.

Separately, on live customer infra, graph/multi-step tests (`YamlNodeExecutor`/`ConditionalGraphExecutor`) were found to have zero `TestPhaseTimer` coverage at all — their per-node HTTP sends are completely untimed, landing in `OTHER` regardless of duration. Not fixed in this PR; worth a follow-up to extend the same timer pattern to that path.

## Dockerfile

Switched mini-testing's base image `eclipse-temurin:17-jre` → `17-jdk` for `jcmd`/`jstack` on customer infra. Known accepted tradeoff: 1 critical + 5 high CVEs more than `-jre` — tolerable until the customer-side RCA is fully closed out.

## Testing

- `mvn -pl libs/utils,apps/mini-testing -am compile` — clean
- Multiple local bench runs and two live customer-infra debugging sessions, correlated across `TESTRUN COST` logs, live `jstack`, JFR (`JavaMonitorEnter`/`ExecutionSample`), and `asprof` wall-clock captures — each fix's effect measured independently before being folded in

title: fix: enforce product-scope NO_ACCESS check regardless of RBAC billing tier
body:
## Summary

Reported symptom: a user without RBAC access to Atlas (Endpoint Security) sees a red "You do not have access to this product. Please ask Admin to grant access or navigate to accessible product" banner and `fetchAgenticUsers` correctly returns 403 — but `fetchAgenticAssetsSummary` on the same page, for the same user, returns real data.

## Root cause

`RoleAccessInterceptor.intercept()` had two genuinely independent checks collapsed behind one early-return:

1. **Billing gate** — `UsageMetricCalculator.isRbacFeatureAvailable(accountId)`: has this account paid for the RBAC/custom-roles add-on? If not, the fine-grained per-feature read/write check should relax to "full access" (there's no custom-role concept to enforce without the add-on).
2. **Product-scope gate** — `Role.NO_ACCESS`: does this *specific user* have any access to this product line (API / AGENTIC / ENDPOINT / MCP / DAST) at all? This is a fundamental per-user boundary, unrelated to the account's billing tier.

The old code checked (1) *before* (2), with an exemption only for the `ADMIN_ACTIONS` featureLabel:

```java
if(!(UsageMetricCalculator.isRbacFeatureAvailable(sessionAccId) || featureLabel.equalsIgnoreCase(Feature.ADMIN_ACTIONS.toString()))){
    return invocation.invoke();   // <-- skips check (2) entirely
}
... // NO_ACCESS check happens after this, so it's skipped along with it
```

So for any account without the RBAC add-on, **every endpoint except the hardcoded `ADMIN_ACTIONS`-labeled ones skipped the NO_ACCESS denial too** — silently leaking product-scoped data to users explicitly denied access to that product.

## Why fetchAgenticUsers/fetchMcpRegistries were fine but fetchAgenticAssetsSummary wasn't

Both `fetchAgenticUsers` (`ModuleInfoAction`) and `fetchMcpRegistries` (`McpAllowlistAction`) are gated by `ADMIN_ACTIONS` — the one hardcoded exemption, always enforced regardless of billing tier. `fetchAgenticAssetsSummary`, like nearly every other endpoint in the codebase, is gated by `API_COLLECTIONS`, which is subject to the bypass.

## This is not a scale-test-PR regression — it's a pre-existing, dormant bug

Confirmed via `git log`:
- `RoleAccessInterceptor.java` was last touched years ago (`add threat access toggle in role`, a string of `product scope changes` commits) — completely untouched by the ATLAS scale-out work. This commit is its first change since.
- `fetchAgenticUsers` and `fetchMcpRegistries`'s struts.xml entries similarly predate the scale-test PR by years.
- `fetchAgenticAssetsSummary` is a *new* endpoint, added by `937bfa384a` ("Rebuild ATLAS agentic pages onto server-side pagination"). Its predecessor — the old Agentic Assets page — fetched its data from `api/getAllCollectionsBasic`, whose struts.xml entry (`API_COLLECTIONS`-gated, confirmed via `git log -S`, last touched in an unrelated 2024-era commit) is *also* untouched by the rebuild.
- Checked whether a separate DAO-level filter (`AccountsContextDaoWithRbac`, applied automatically to every `ApiCollectionsDao.findAll` call) might have been compensating on the old page. It scopes queries by `UsersCollectionsList.getCollectionsIdForUser`/`getContextCollectionsForUser` — a "which collections belong to this product/role-group" filter, not a "does this user have any right to query this product at all" check. It applies identically to old and new code, so it wouldn't have caught this on either.

**Conclusion**: the old page's primary data source (`getAllCollectionsBasic`) had this exact same gap the whole time. The rebuild didn't introduce the vulnerability — it introduced a new endpoint that happened to inherit the same already-broken gate every non-`ADMIN_ACTIONS` endpoint has always had. This most likely surfaced now because this specific test scenario (a NO_ACCESS-scoped test user, checked directly against this page's data) hadn't been run against either version of the page before.

## Fix

Reordered so the NO_ACCESS product-scope check runs unconditionally whenever `DashboardMode.isMetered()` — independent of the RBAC billing gate. The billing gate now only relaxes the fine-grained per-feature check that follows it, which is what it was actually meant to do. Pure reorder, no new logic, no message/behavior changes for either check individually.

## Test plan
- [x] Compiles clean; dashboard restarts cleanly with no new errors.
- [x] **Confirmed live by the reporter**: fix resolves the reported leak.
- [x] Confirmed via code trace this is a no-op for any account with the RBAC add-on already granted (the common path) — no regression risk there.
- [x] Confirmed via git history this is a long-standing gap, not something introduced by the ATLAS scale-out PR (see RCA above).

## Why
Customer log showed ~100 occurrences in a 16-minute window of:
\`error extracting response in fetchTestScript java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "com.mongodb.BasicDBObject.toJson()" because "testScriptObj" is null\`

Root cause: \`TestScriptsDao.fetchTestScript()\` (server-side) legitimately returns \`null\` whenever the account has no \`TestScript\` configured for that type — the common case, not an error. The server serializes that as \`testScript: null\`, but \`ClientActor.fetchTestScript()\` unconditionally called \`.toJson()\` on it, NPEing on every such normal response. Caught by the outer try/catch and logged as ERROR each time — since scripts are cached with a 5-min TTL (\`ApiExecutorUtil.getCachedScript\`), this fires on essentially every cache refresh for any account/type without a configured script.

## What
Guard on \`testScriptObj == null\` and skip the parse — \`testScript\` stays \`null\`, which is already the correct/handled "no script" case downstream.

body:
## Why
Test runs were slow: persisting each finished result took up to 5 sequential HTTP calls to
cyborg (insert, count update, issue lookup, issue write, issue count update), and two
completely separate call sites (`FilterAction.isAgenticCollection`,
`McpSseEndpointHelper.addSseEndpointHeader`) were independently re-fetching the same API
collection metadata from cyborg on nearly every single test, uncached.

## What
- Adds a consolidated `bulkRecordTestingRunResults` call (server side in the companion cyborg
  PR) that does insert + issue-write in one round trip instead of up to 5. Gated behind
  `USE_BULK_RECORD_TESTING_RUN_RESULTS` so the old per-call flow stays available.
- Adds a shared `ApiCollectionMetaCache` so both of the previously-uncached call sites above
  hit the network once per distinct collection ID instead of once per test.

## Result
Verified via real benchmark runs against production-scale data (205 APIs, 137k tests,
concurrency=200, real cyborg): ~90/s baseline → ~180/s after the bulk-write change → ~219/s

title: Add consolidated bulkRecordTestingRunResults API to database-abstractor
body:
## Why

Investigated a customer report of test runs taking hours. Traced part of the slowdown to how mini-testing persists each finished test result: for every single `(API, test)` outcome, it makes up to **5-7 separate HTTP calls** to database-abstractor (insert result, update run-summary counts, look up existing issues, write issue updates, update issue counts, plus conditional calls for reruns/custom templates) — each its own network round trip, each individually exposed to retries/backoff if the backend hiccups. Profiling showed this persistence tail was 67-76% of the measured per-test cost, well above actual test-execution time.

## What

Adds one new endpoint, `bulkRecordTestingRunResults`, that does all of that work for a batch of results in a single call. It's a straight port of the existing per-result logic (same business rules, same Mongo documents, same semantics) — not a redesign — just collapsed from N round trips into 1.

This PR is intentionally scoped to **just the new endpoint**: nothing existing is modified. No existing route, action method, or `DataActor`/`DbLayer` method changed — this is purely additive, so it can't regress anything currently in production. The mini-testing side (actually calling this instead of the old per-result flow) is a separate, follow-up change — this PR only adds the capability.

## Test plan

- [x] Compiles clean (`libs/dao`, `libs/utils`, `apps/database-abstractor`).
- [x] Isolated benchmark (new endpoint vs. the equivalent old per-result calls, same payload, same local Mongo): consolidating to one call was ~2x faster even on localhost with no real network latency — expected to be a bigger win in production where each old round trip pays real WAN/hybrid latency.
- [x] Manually verified via the local benchmark harness that a passing/first-seen result persists correctly through the new endpoint.
- [ ] Deploy to a shared non-prod environment (doesn't touch existing APIs, so safe to deploy ahead of any caller using it) and run mini-testing locally against it with the caller-side change, to verify the less-common paths end-to-end:
  - a genuinely new vulnerability creates its issue document (this path had a real bug, since fixed - see commit history)
  - an existing issue's `collectionIds` survive a repeat update (also previously buggy, since fixed)
  - run-summary counts (`testResultsCount`, `countIssues`) come out correct after a mixed batch of passing/vulnerable results
  - a rerun-replace (`rerunDeleteIds`) correctly deletes the prior result

> Recreated from #6155, which GitHub locked closed after the branch history was rewritten to remove an accidentally-committed secret. Same branch, same base, secret scrubbed from history.

**Fix: infinite loop in `resolveWordListVar` when a word list is empty**

Fills `${blanks}` with values, returns every combination:
```
"${color} ${animal}"  color=[red,blue] animal=[cat,dog] → ["red cat","red dog","blue cat","blue dog"]
```

Bug — when `animal=[]`:
```
find ${animal} → for(v : []) {}      // empty list, nothing replaced
                                     // ${animal} still in the string
re-scan same string → find ${animal} → for(v : []) {}
re-scan same string → find ${animal} → ...forever (100% CPU until 300s timeout)
```
Replacing a blank is what removes its `${…}`; an empty list never replaces, so `${animal}` stays and is re-found every pass.

Trigger: `sample_data` word lists (e.g. `accountValues`) on APIs whose payload lacks those fields → empty list. ~2% of tests, capping throughput at ~20/s.

Fix: empty list → no combination possible → return empty instead of re-scanning.

Agent SDK — Phase 1: canonical contract + characterization safety net
body:
## The problem

Every agent connector is a copy-pasted bundle with no tests. The same logic is duplicated per agent and has drifted (`akto_machine_id.py`: 9 copies; `akto-hooks.py`: 7). Drift has already shipped bugs.

```
BEFORE  — 6 connectors, each a self-contained copy, zero tests
  claude-cli-hooks/   gemini-cli-hooks/   codex-cli-hooks/   cursor-hooks/  ...(x6)
    akto-validate-*.py      # payload + guardrail logic — copied per agent
    akto-hooks.py           # copied x7 (drifted)
    akto_machine_id.py      # copied x9 (drifted)
    *-wrapper.sh / *.ps1    # copied per hook (env exports + exec)
    settings.json

AFTER   — one tested SDK; per-agent code is a thin, hidden adapter
  agent_sdk/                     # shared engine — written & tested ONCE
    contract.py                  #   typed model (Turn, Decision, ...)
    engine/                      #   ids, transport, enforcement, device id, ...
    adapters/<agent>_adapter.py  #   ~30 lines per agent, hidden
  business_logic/build_akto_payload.py   # the one thing that changes often
  manifests/<agent>.toml                 # tiny, per agent
  ~/.akto/config.json                    # replaces per-agent wrapper env
```

`SPEC.md` in this PR describes the full plan; migration is phased and keeps the backend untouched.

## This PR = Phase 1 only (foundation, no behavior change)

- Adds the typed **contract** (`contract.py`).
- Adds **characterization tests** that pin the *current* output of the existing shared code, so later phases can move/dedupe it and prove nothing changed.
- Changes **no existing file** — tests import current code read-only. Verified on the Python 3.8 floor (16/16).

Later phases move the duplicated logic behind the contract and delete the copies.

Fix "Access Restricted" gate blocking open-source local_deploy dashboards
body:
### Problem

On a self-hosted open-source deployment (`DASHBOARD_MODE=local_deploy`, not SaaS), the dashboard shows **"Access Restricted / Contact Sales"** after a successful login, instead of the API Inventory. Reported in #5512.

### Root cause

The SPA access gate in `apps/main/index.js` grants access only when `window.PLAN_TYPE ∈ {enterprise, professional, trial}`:

```js
if(window.PLAN_TYPE && ALLOWED_PLANS.includes(window.PLAN_TYPE.toLowerCase())) {
  free = false;
} else {
  free = true; // blocked
}
```

`PLAN_TYPE` is resolved via the billing service, which does not exist on a self-hosted box, so on a fresh `local_deploy` login `window.PLAN_TYPE === ""` while `window.DASHBOARD_MODE === "LOCAL_DEPLOY"`. The gate never consults `DASHBOARD_MODE`/`IS_SAAS`, so the open-source user is blocked.

### Fix

Treat `local_deploy` / non-SaaS deployments as never-paywalled by adding them to the existing bypass condition (alongside whitelisted orgs and signup pages). No effect on SaaS behavior.

### Testing

Reproduced on `2.19.0_local` (also reported on `2.8.5_local`): fresh signup + login → "Access Restricted". With this change, `local_deploy` logins route straight to the dashboard and all OSS features (API Discovery, Testing, Reports) are accessible.

Fixes #5512

title: Fix NPE on first-user email signup (null scopeRoleMapping)
body:
### Problem

On a fresh self-hosted deployment, creating the **first user via email signup** fails with a 500:

```
java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.util.Map.put(Object, Object)" because "this.scopeRoleMapping" is null
    at com.akto.action.SignupAction.createUserAndRedirect(SignupAction.java:1520)
```

### Root cause

`createUserAndRedirect()` assumes `this.scopeRoleMapping` is non-null in the new-org (`newOrgSetup`) branch and calls `.put(...)` on it directly:

```java
} else {
    this.scopeRoleMapping.put("API", RBAC.Role.ADMIN.name());   // NPE when null
    ...
}
```

But `registerViaEmail()` only initializes `scopeRoleMapping` for the **pending-invite** path. For a brand-new org's first user (no invite), it reaches `createUserAndRedirect(...)` with `scopeRoleMapping` still `null`.

The SSO signup paths (Google/GitHub/Azure) are unaffected because they go through `createUserAndRedirectWithDefaultRole()`, which initializes the map first — which is why only **email** first-user signup breaks.

### Fix

Guard the map before assigning the default ADMIN scopes in the `newOrgSetup` branch (one localized null-check; no behavior change for existing callers).

### Testing

Reproduced on a clean `mongo` volume: first email signup returned 500 with the NPE above. After the patch, the first user is created with an ADMIN RBAC (`API/ENDPOINT/DAST/AGENTIC → ADMIN`) and can log in normally.

fix: stop bouncing Atlas device drill-downs off /inventory before the endpoint tree can render
body:
## Summary
- `5d32fc2068` (already on master) made `/dashboard/observe/inventory` unconditionally redirect Atlas to `/dashboard/observe/agentic-assets`.
- Atlas's own left-nav never targets `/inventory` directly — but `UsersAndDevices.jsx`'s row click does: it stores a device/agent filter under `INVENTORY_FILTER_KEY` and *then* navigates here, so this page can render that device's endpoint tree (`AgentEndpointTreeTable`, gated by `useTreeView`).
- The unconditional redirect skipped that tree every time and bounced straight to the grouped assets page instead, discarding the filter/context — "clicking any endpoint" appeared to just redirect away instead of showing the tree it used to show.
- Fix: only redirect when there's no such filter present (i.e. a stale link/bookmark, not a device drill-down).

**Follow-up (2nd commit)**: once the redirect was fixed, the drill-down still called `api.getAllCollectionsBasic()` on mount — loading every collection in the whole account just to filter it down to one device's handful client-side. body:
## Summary

Investigated a user report that PRs #6020/#6021/#6029's "skills shouldn't pollute violation
counts" fixes were lost during a merge. They were — but the underlying page had also been
rebuilt onto server-side aggregation in the meantime, so restoring the original client-side diffs
verbatim wouldn't have done anything (the functions they patched have zero live callers today).
This finds and fixes the actual current-architecture equivalent of the same gap:

- `ThreatActorService.fetchHostSeverityCounts` — the method backing `AgenticAssetsPage.jsx`,
  `DeviceEndpoints.jsx`, and `EndpointPosture.jsx`'s violation counts — was missing the
  `ThreatUtils.excludeSkillEndpointFilter` call every sibling method in the same file already
  has. Skill-invocation (`/skills/<name>`) events were bleeding into every agent/device's own
  violation total. On a real test account, **75% of all malicious events (29.5k/39.1k) were
  skill-invocation events being miscounted this way.**
- Even with that excluded, skills had no way to show their *own* violation count — a skill's
  declaring collection is shared with the agent/device that invoked it, so collection-based
  attribution can never isolate a skill's own events. Added a skill-name-keyed equivalent:
  - New `FetchSkillSeverityCountsRequest/Response` proto messages (mirrors
    `FetchHostSeverityCounts*` but keyed by skill name instead of host)
  - `ThreatActorService.fetchSkillSeverityCounts` — groups `malicious_events` by the skill name
    extracted from each event's `/skills/<name>` endpoint
  - New `/get_skill_severity_counts` router endpoint
  - `ThreatApiAction.fetchSkillSeverityCounts` (dashboard-side client, mirrors
    `fetchHostSeverityCounts`)
  - `AgenticObserveAction`: new `skillViolationsByName` param, used for skill-type rows in both
    `fetchAgenticAssetsSummary`'s per-row violations and `fetchAgenticAssetsStats`' "Top Assets
    with Violations" ranking (agent/service/LLM rows keep using the existing collection-based path)
  - `AgenticAssetsPage.jsx`: fetches the new endpoint alongside the existing host-severity one,
    threads `skillViolationsByName` through to both summary and stats calls

- [x] Verified a skill row's own `violations` field in `fetchAgenticAssetsSummary`'s response

added mini-runtime support to edit envs
body:
## Problem

An account can run many mini-runtime instances. Today, changing a mini-runtime env var (log level, Kafka config, debug filters) means editing every instance's deployment config and restarting each one by hand — there's no way to change a value once and have it apply fleet-wide.

## Why

Fill a value once in the dashboard, every mini-runtime instance for that account picks it up — no per-instance deployment edits.

## Flow

```
User edits env vars in Module Info UI (mini-runtime row)
        │
        ▼
POST /api/updateRuntimeEnvOverrides  ──▶  AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides (Mongo, one doc per account)
        │
        ▼
POST /api/rebootModules (active MINI_RUNTIME instances only)
        │
        ▼
ModuleInfo.reboot = true  ──▶  existing heartbeat mechanism picks it up (~30s) ──▶ instance restarts
```

Two read paths for the UI itself:
```
Module Info table  ◀── ModuleInfo.additionalData.env  (real, per-instance values, reported every heartbeat)
Env editor modal   ──▶ writes to AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides (account-wide, not per-instance)
```

## What's in this PR

- New `AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides` field + `api/updateRuntimeEnvOverrides` endpoint (per-key merge, not whole-map replace).
- `MINI_RUNTIME` added to the Module Info page's configurable module types, reusing the existing per-module env editor UI/component as-is.
- `MINI_RUNTIME` added to `rebootModules`'s allowed-module filter — without this, instances named via `MINI_RUNTIME_NAME` (not the `Default_`/`akto-mr` fallback) never actually got rebooted.
- Env editor now only submits changed keys, so an untouched field can't accidentally overwrite a real value with blank.

Companion PRs (same feature): mini-runtime side https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6025, cyborg side https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6018

## Verified

5 concurrent mini-runtime instances: saved `DEBUG_URLS`/`DEBUG_HOSTS` from this UI, confirmed live pickup within ~30s with no restart; saved `AKTO_LOG_LEVEL`, confirmed all active instances rebooted and the fresh boot reflected the new value.

title: added config handler
body:
## Problem

Mini-runtime only reads config from the container's own environment variables. Changing something like `DEBUG_URLS` or `AKTO_LOG_LEVEL` means editing every instance's deployment and restarting each one by hand — no central place to change a value once for a whole fleet.

## Why

Let select env vars be overridden from the DB (`AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides`, written from the dashboard — see PR #6026), so ops can change them once instead of per-instance.

## Flow (as currently implemented)

```
AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides (Mongo)
        │  polled every 30s (+ once synchronously at boot) by ConfigHandler
        ▼
   ConfigHandler.overrides (in-memory map)
        │
        ▼
   readEnv(name, default): DB override → System.getenv → default
        │
        ▼
   Read at class-load / process start only (Main.java, LoggerMaker.java, Utils.java field init)
        │
        ▼
   New value takes effect only after the next restart of that instance
```

Every heartbeat, mini-runtime also reports its current values for these vars into `ModuleInfo.additionalData.env` — the same mechanism other module types (threat-detection, traffic-collector) already use — so the dashboard's Module Info page can show real per-instance state instead of guessing.

## What's in this PR

- New `ConfigHandler`: polls `AccountSettings.runtimeEnvOverrides`, exposes `readEnv(name, default)`.
- `DEBUG_URLS`/`DEBUG_HOSTS` (`Utils.java`) and `AKTO_LOG_LEVEL`, `MINI_RUNTIME_NAME`, `AKTO_CONFIG_NAME`, `AKTO_KAFKA_BROKER_URL`, `AKTO_KAFKA_GROUP_ID_CONFIG`, `AKTO_KAFKA_MAX_POLL_RECORDS_CONFIG` (`Main.java`, `LoggerMaker.java`) now read through `ConfigHandler` instead of `System.getenv` directly.
- `ModuleInfoWorker` reports the whitelisted env values on every heartbeat.
- Deliberately narrow: only these vars, not a blanket `System.getenv` replacement. `VPC_ID` and `DB_MERGING_MODE` were considered and excluded — too load-bearing to convert without more scrutiny.

Companion PRs (same feature): dashboard side https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6026, cyborg side https://github.com/akto-api-security/akto/pull/6018

Add v2 browser-extension config API (rich, typed extraction spec)
body:
## What

Adds `fetchBrowserExtensionConfigsV2` to the database-abstractor — the endpoint the browser extension calls to load per-site monitoring configs.

- Serves the account-level configs, now carrying the **full extraction spec** the extension supports: `transport, method, format, path, operations, frameMatch, responseFormat, responsePath(s), responseKeyPath, modelPath, modelHeader, triggerFrame, blockResponseFrames, identity, enforceAt`.
- These fields are **polymorphic** (`path`/`modelPath`/`responsePath` are a String *or* a List), so the read maps raw documents via `BrowserExtensionConfigCommon.fromDocument` instead of the POJO codec. This yields a typed object that exposes **only known config fields** — the account row's `createdBy`/`updatedBy` audit/PII never leaks to this public-facing endpoint.
- `BrowserExtensionConfigCommon` extended to model the remaining extension fields (`identity`, `responseFormat`/`responsePath`/`responsePaths`/`responseKeyPath`, `modelPath`/`modelHeader`, `triggerFrame`, `blockResponseFrames`, `enforceAt`).

## Paired with

Dashboard-side changes (catalogue→account spec copy on enable, tolerant read) in akto-api-security/akto#5956.

## Test

`POST /api/fetchBrowserExtensionConfigsV2` returns each active host with its full spec and **no** `createdBy`/`updatedBy`.

- Open `/dashboard/settings/browser-extension`: configured list loads (no duplicate rows), toggle on/off persists, add/edit custom host works, version tooltip renders.

feat: cap logs_endpoint_shield and align indexes with master
body:
## What
Port the endpoint-shield log capping + index cleanup from master (`a104c00576`) to this job-runner branch.

- `logs_endpoint_shield` is now created as / converted to a **100 MB capped collection**, guarded by `DbMode.allowCappedCollections()` (DocumentDB/Cosmos fall back to a plain collection).
- Reduced to a **single `{agentId, key, _id}` index**, matching master. Dropped the previously-created `{timestamp}`, `{agentId}` and `{deviceId}` indexes to cut write amplification on this high-write collection.

## Why this branch
These branches run the jobs (`AKTO_RUN_JOB`) that perform DAO init / `createIndices` in production; they do **not** serve the dashboard APIs. So the index set they create must match what the API-serving dashboard (master) queries — hence porting master's index set verbatim.

## Notes
- **DAO-only** change. No `EndpointShieldAgentAction` change (these branches don't serve that query) and no Liquibase migration (the `account/` changelog dir doesn't exist on this branch).
- The key field is referenced by the string literal `"key"` instead of `EndpointShieldLog.KEY`, because `Log.KEY` isn't present on all of these branches; the resulting index is byte-identical to master's.
- `convertToCapped` on an existing large collection performs a locking server-side clone (and drops non-`_id` indexes, which are then rebuilt) — roll out in a maintenance window.
